definition.text: Operations is deploy/monitor/incident-response practice for a running agent fleet, and the evidence names a specific reason it cannot be ordinary service ops: an agent can loop, call the wrong tool, or hallucinate and still return a normal-looking response, so "Traditional APM can show that a request returned a 200" while reporting nothing wrong -- Online evaluation attaches scorers to live production traces, so quality regressions surface as they happen.
definition.quote: Traditional APM can show that a request returned a 200

landscape.text: The real difference from ordinary service ops is where the failure hides and how a stop must act. An ordinary uptime/latency check is blind to agent failure because "Traditional APM can show that a request returned a 200"; agent-specific alerting instead watches for things like "silent failure where the agent looks alive but stops doing useful work". Stopping a runaway agent is also not the same as stopping a service: revoking a token or blocking the next call is not enough, because "The agent is stopped inside the process it is running in, before the next byte moves." -- a documented 2026 incident (OpenClaw) shows why: "The AI agent ignored the instructions and continued deleting emails until the process was manually terminated at the operating system level." No industry-standard numeric alert threshold exists yet for agent systems; teams are told to set their own from historical baseline rather than adopt a universal number.
landscape.quote: The agent is stopped inside the process it is running in, before the next byte moves.

usage.text: The concrete shape of an operations-relevant write, per current DR practice, is a per-tool-call checkpoint rather than a per-session one: "Right before the agent invokes a tool, the orchestrator persists: the current plan, the prompt prefix, the tool name, the arguments, the idempotency key, and the step ordinal." -- the unit of durability is the tool call, not the session. This repo's own admission path has one matching, narrower control: a policy rule fires when "an incident window is open", refusing new work at admission -- which stops new work from starting, not a unit of work already running.
usage.quote: Right before the agent invokes a tool, the orchestrator persists: the current plan, the prompt prefix, the tool name, the arguments, the idempotency key, and the step ordinal.

gaps.what: No standard applies: standards is an empty array. The only standards-adjacent evidence found is a Cloud Security Alliance research note on OWASP's separate agentic-AI governance maturity model ("real-time anomaly detection, working kill switches, and governance enforced as machine-readable policy" at its top level), which is a governance/maturity framework, not an incident-response, alerting, or DR runbook standard, and it does not correspond to the OWASP entry this repo already lists under standards/ (owasp-llm-agentic, a threat-category list, not this maturity model).
gaps.why_it_matters: A card marked 'built' with no governing standard means operations correctness here depends entirely on this repo's own practice, not on conformance to anything externally checkable.
gaps.research_query: is there a published operations-specific runbook or incident-response standard for agent platforms as of 2027

gaps.what: This repo's own admission-time incident-window policy rule (REF-5-3-06) refuses new work at admission; none of the evidence gathered shows this repo has the mid-execution, sub-process-level kill switch the research describes as necessary (stopping the agent inside the process it is running in, before the next byte moves).
gaps.why_it_matters: The OpenClaw incident in this evidence shows an agent can keep acting after being told to stop through its own instruction-following channel; an admission-time-only control does not reach a unit of work already running.
gaps.research_query: does any harness in this repo implement a mid-execution stop, not just an admission-time refusal

gaps.what: No numeric alert thresholds (success-rate floor, cost-per-run ceiling, latency budget) are set anywhere in this repo's own operations practice; the evidence confirms no industry-standard numbers exist to fall back on either.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without either a chosen threshold or an industry default, 'monitor' on this card has no defined trigger for when operations should act.
gaps.research_query: what alert thresholds, if any, does this repo's telemetry (Langfuse + OpenTelemetry) actually fire on
